hook: Open a map app to find a pizza place and you see streets and names: where things are. Open a weather page and you see colored bands of temperature: what conditions are like. Both are maps of the same ground, made for different jobs. Every map is a choice about what to show, what to leave out, and how to flatten a round Earth onto a flat screen.

prereq.q: A legend's classes run from "Under 40%" to "80% or more". What does the legend tell you?
options: What each shade on the map stands for
Who made the data and when
How far apart places are on the ground
The scale of analysis of the map
prereq.why: A legend says what each shade, symbol or line means. The source line gives who and when.

prereq.q: Which map is the large-scale map?
prereq.why: Large scale means a large fraction: things look big and the area shown is small.

figure.caption: The same invented island drawn as a reference map and as five kinds of thematic map.

chain.cause: The Earth is round and a map is flat
chain.effect: every map projection distorts shape, area, distance or direction

chain.cause: A map maker chooses one property to keep true
chain.effect: other properties are stretched, so each projection suits some jobs and not others

chain.cause: A thematic map shows one measure across places
chain.effect: the map type (shades, dots, symbols, lines) decides which pattern you can see

ideas: A reference map shows where things are (borders, cities, roads). A thematic map shows one topic or measure across places.

Thematic types: a choropleth map shades areas by a rate or class; a dot density map shows counts as dots; a graduated symbol map sizes symbols by amount; an isoline map joins points of equal value; a cartogram resizes areas by a value.
A map projection flattens the globe and always causes distortion of shape, area, distance or direction. Choosing one is a trade-off.
Absolute distance and direction use kilometers and the compass; relative distance and direction depend on time, cost or the viewer. Maps also show clustering, dispersal and elevation.

misconception.wrong: There is one correct world map that shows the Earth as it really is.
misconception.right: Every flat map distorts something. A map that keeps areas true stretches shapes, and one that keeps shapes true inflates areas toward the poles. The right projection depends on the job.

summary: Maps are tools with jobs. Reference maps show where things are; thematic maps show a measure, using shades, dots, sized symbols, lines of equal value or resized areas. Every projection distorts shape, area, distance or direction, so choosing one is a trade-off. Maps show absolute and relative distance and direction, clustering and dispersal, and elevation.
